lessons.title: 1. One cable, two directions

steps.say: One USB cable joins the CQ and the Mac, and it carries sound both ways at once. First the way from the mixer to the computer. Sixteen channels.

Channels one to ten are your ten inputs, each on its own channel. Whatever comes into input one, a microphone or a recording, goes to the computer on channel one. Ableton can record all ten at once, one track each.

Channels eleven to sixteen are three stereo pairs, and you choose what they carry. Now they carry the ST IN channel, the outputs five and six, and the main mix. That choice is the page you did not understand: CONFIG, the USB tab, Channel Assignment. It only decides what is sent to the computer.
Here it is. Eleven twelve, ST IN. Thirteen fourteen, outputs five and six. Fifteen sixteen, the main mix. Read these three boxes as: what do I want to record on the computer on these channels.

manual.q: Mono input channels are permanently assigned to USB/SD outputs.

lessons.title: 2. From the computer back to the mixer

steps.say: The other direction. The computer also sends sixteen channels back to the mixer. In Ableton they are called Ext. Out, one to sixteen.

Ext. Out one to ten play on inputs one to ten, but only when the input's source is set to SD and USB. With the source on analogue, the input listens to the socket on the back instead. For the Santoshi concert all ten are on SD and USB, so the ten recorded musicians play on your ten faders, exactly as if they were on stage.
You see it on every input: the small SD and USB picture.

manual.q: select USB/SD to source from USB drive and SD card.
manual.from: CQ User Guide › CONFIG screens › Inputs › Input Source

steps.say: The manual says, in the CONFIG chapter: select USB and SD to source from USB drive and SD card.

manual.q: the source will be the SD Card, otherwise it will be USB-B.
manual.from: CQ User Guide › CONFIG screens › Inputs › Input Source

steps.say: The manual says, in the CONFIG chapter: the source will be the SD Card, otherwise it will be USB B.

Channels eleven to sixteen coming back are fixed, and I measured them by watching the meters. Ext. Out eleven and twelve play on the ST IN channel. Thirteen and fourteen play on the channel called USB. Fifteen and sixteen did not show on any channel. So for a stereo sound from the computer you have two places: ST IN, or USB.

manual.from: CQ User Guide › HOME screens › USB

steps.say: The manual says, in the HOME chapter: Stereo USB playback signal will be sent to the dedicated stereo USB Input channel.

lessons.title: 3. How everything is routed right now

steps.say: The whole picture, as it is right now. On the left, Ableton plays the Santoshi concert. Ten tracks go out on Ext. Out one to ten, into the ten inputs of the CQ. They are shaped in processing, mixed with the faders, and summed into the main mix.
The main mix goes through the main compressor, to the speakers, and to the SD card when you record.

At the bottom, the venue's own stereo mix, recorded at the concert. It is one stereo file, so I made two tracks of it in Live. Venue L, panned fully left, goes to Ext. Out thirteen. Venue R, panned fully right, goes to fourteen. Together they arrive in stereo on the USB channel. The two tracks play the same clip, so they are always in sync.
The USB fader stays down at off. So the venue sound never enters your main mix and never reaches the SD recording. You hear it only through the listen key, in the headphones.

lessons.title: 4. The USB preview while you record

steps.say: Lesson four, the first project. You record your mix to the SD card, and at the same time you compare it with the mix the venue made. The recording takes the main mix. The headphones take whatever listen key is pressed. Those are two separate roads, so pressing listen never changes the recording.

This is the listen key of the USB channel. Pressed, your headphones play the venue mix. Released, they play your main mix. Go back and forth during a whole song. Where is your voice clearer, where is theirs? Where is your bass bigger? Listening like this teaches more than any book.

manual.from: CQ User Guide › FADER screens › Listen

steps.say: The manual says, in the FADER chapter: Touch the listen button to hear only that channel in the headphone output.
Recording is on the HOME page, RECORD. Start it at the first song and stop it after the last. The listen key does not touch what is recorded.

lessons.title: 5. Preparing the concert in Live: names, markers, -12 dB

steps.say: Before any mixing, the recording is prepared in Live. Three things: names, markers, and the level of every channel. This preparation comes before every mix you will ever do.

Names. The concert came from the Windows computer with tracks called one audio, two audio, and so on. The recording mixer at the concert, the Behringer, had a label on every input, like svemir VOC or tajana. I read which input each track recorded, and gave each track that name. Live can be told the names over a small network door called OSC, so I did not type them by hand. The three percussion channels had unclear labels, so I listened to them with a sound analysis, and you named them: mridangam, mridangam low and djembe.

Markers. Up here are eight locators, one at the start of each song, from Jai Ganesha to Asatoma. To find them, I measured the venue mix for the quiet gaps between songs, and then let the speech recogniser listen to the first words after each gap, to confirm which song begins there. Then the eight locators were written into the Live set at those times. Now one click jumps to any song.

And the most important: the level. Most channels of this recording touched the very top, zero decibels. So I measured every clip: I cut it into tenths of a second, took the peak of each, and found the level that ninety nine percent of those peaks stay under. That is the typical peak. Then I set each clip's gain so that its typical peak sits at minus twelve decibels. Every track fader in Live stays at zero.

The result: every channel reaches the mixer at the same level, with twelve decibels of room above it for the loud moments. Every fader on the CQ now starts from the same place. Do this first, every time you bring in a new multitrack. Then mix.

lessons.title: 6. Theory: gain staging, the level before the mix

steps.say: Mixing theory begins before any fader: the level that arrives. Every channel should arrive at the same working level, with space above it for the loud moments. That space is called headroom.

In the Santoshi recordings most channels already hit the very top, zero decibels, and the two mridangam microphones even clipped at the concert. That distortion is in the files and cannot be removed. So in Live I set each clip so that its typical peak is at minus twelve. Every channel now reaches the CQ at the same level, with twelve decibels of headroom.

Why peak and not loudness? A drum is short and spiky. Made as loud as a voice, its spikes would go over the top and distort again. Levelling by the typical peak keeps every spike under the ceiling. And because all channels start equal, every fader on the CQ starts from the same place, and the mix is only about balance.

lessons.title: 7. Theory: equaliser and the high pass filter

steps.say: The equaliser. Every instrument fills a part of the frequency range, from the deep bass on the left to the air on the right. A mix is clear when instruments do not fight for the same place.

The first tool is the high pass filter. It removes everything below a chosen frequency. A voice has nothing useful below about a hundred hertz, only stage rumble, breath and handling noise. Cutting it makes room for the bass and the low drum. That is why every vocal channel has its HPF on, the green badge on each strip.
Between two hundred and four hundred hertz lives the mud. When many voices and guitars add up there, the mix sounds thick and unclear. A small cut there on guitars often lets the voices through.
Between two and five thousand hertz lives presence, where words become understandable. A voice that is lost in the mix often needs a little more here, not more fader.

For Santoshi I did not draw these curves by hand. I listened to each channel and chose the CQ's Quick preset that fits it: vocal low pitch for Svemir and Igor, vocal high pitch for Tajana, clean bass, acoustic guitar, and percussion presets for mridangam and djembe. A preset is a good start; your ears decide the rest.

lessons.title: 8. Theory: the compressor on each channel

steps.say: The compressor. A voice in a concert goes from a whisper to a shout. A compressor turns the loud moments down automatically, so the soft and the strong words come closer together, and the voice stays in front without riding the fader all night.
Four settings. The threshold is the level where it starts working. Below it, nothing happens.

manual.q: Adjust the input level at which compression will be active.
manual.from: CQ User Guide › PROCESSING screens › Compressor › Threshold

steps.say: The manual says, in the PROCESSING chapter: Adjust the input level at which compression will be active.
The ratio is how strongly it turns down above the threshold. Two to one means: for every two decibels louder that come in, only one comes out.

manual.q: The ratio of the incoming signal to compressed signal when compression is active.
manual.from: CQ User Guide › PROCESSING screens › Compressor › Ratio

steps.say: The manual says, in the PROCESSING chapter: The ratio of the incoming signal to compressed signal when compression is active.

The attack is how fast it reacts, the release how fast it lets go. A slow attack lets the first hit of a drum or a consonant through, so the sound stays alive. A fast attack catches everything, and can make it flat.

manual.q: the time it takes for compression to take effect
manual.from: CQ User Guide › PROCESSING screens › Compressor › Attack

steps.say: The manual says, in the PROCESSING chapter: the time it takes for compression to take effect.

manual.q: the time that it takes for the compressor to stop compressing
manual.from: CQ User Guide › PROCESSING screens › Compressor › Release

steps.say: The manual says, in the PROCESSING chapter: the time that it takes for the compressor to stop compressing.
Each Santoshi channel's preset carries a gentle compressor made for that instrument: steady for voices, quicker for percussion, so the mridangam's hits stay crisp but do not jump out.

lessons.title: 9. Theory: reverb on a send

steps.say: Reverb. A dry voice sounds close and small. A little reverb puts it in a room. On the CQ the reverb is a shared effect unit. Each channel sends a copy of itself into it, and the reverb comes back into the main mix.
That is better than putting the reverb on each channel, because all voices share the same room, and the reverb has one fader of its own.

For Santoshi, effect unit one is easy verb, type Vocal Classic. Only the three voices send to it, Svemir, Igor and Tajana, each at about minus thirteen. Drums and bass send nothing: reverb on them would blur the rhythm.
To change a send: Sends To, FX one, and the faders become the amounts going into the reverb. Sends To, Main LR, to come back.

manual.q: select an FX to show all send levels to that FX unit on the fader
manual.from: CQ User Guide › FADER screens › Sends to an FX

steps.say: The manual says, in the FADER chapter: select an FX to show all send levels to that FX unit on the fader.

lessons.title: 10. Theory: the glue compressor on the main

steps.say: The glue. One more compressor sits on the whole main mix. It is set very gently, so it never squashes, it only holds the parts together, like glue. When the whole band plays loud it pulls back a little, and the mix breathes as one.

These are the Santoshi settings. RMS, so it follows the average loudness and not every spike. Soft knee, so it starts gradually. Ratio one point nine to one, gentle. Threshold minus fourteen point four, so it only works in the loud parts. Attack twenty five milliseconds, slow enough to let the hits of the drums through. Release about one hundred and eighty milliseconds, so it lets go in time with the music. Gain zero, nothing added.
Watch the main meter during the loudest song. If the compressor works all the time, raise the threshold. If it never moves, that is fine too: a glue you cannot hear is a good glue.

lessons.title: 11. Balancing the Santoshi mix

steps.say: The balance, the real mixing. In devotional music the voices carry the meaning, so the order is: voices first, then rhythm, then colour.
I play Jai Ganesha and solo Svemir's voice in Live. Bring his fader to about zero. Listen: clear, no rumble, steady.

Solo off. Now bring Igor and Tajana until the three voices sit together, none under and none over. Then the mridangam, the low mridangam and the djembe, until the rhythm carries the voices without covering them. Then bass and guitars, felt more than heard. If the voices turn muddy, the bass or the guitars are too loud.

Watch the main meter: the loudest moments near zero, never red. If everything is too loud, bring all faders down together, never the main above zero. Then compare with the venue mix on the USB listen key, and when you are happy, store it: HOME, SCENES, Santoshi Mix, Overwrite.

lessons.title: 12. Book: Know the sound before you start

steps.say: Before you touch a fader, the book asks you to know what the mix should sound like. A few words are enough to start: warm, open, close. The idea may change on the way, but without one you wander.
For Santoshi, try three words: warm, natural, and the words clear. It is devotional music. The listener should feel inside the kirtan, not in a pop studio.
The book also says every style of music has its own habits, and they are there for a reason. Acoustic music wants warmth. And it wants natural spaces, like a room or a hall, not strange effects.
That is why effect one is easy verb, type Vocal Classic: a natural room around the voices. And no special effects on the drums.
Another picture from the book: the mix is a film. Some parts play the leading role and get the close-ups. Others support them, some appear now and then, and some fill the background.
In Santoshi the leading roles are the three voices: Tajana, Svemir and Igor. They stay near the middle and in front. In a kirtan the voices answer each other, so the lead passes from one to the next.

The mridangam, both heads, and the bass carry the pulse: the supporting roles. The guitars and the djembe are colour around the voices. Igor's guitar moves from the DI to the microphone in the second half, but it is the same role, so it keeps the same place. The reverb is the background: you hardly notice it, but without it the voices sound small.

book.q: Your mix tells a story, just like a movie
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 2: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Five Best Practices › 2.1 Have a Concept

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Five Best Practices: Your mix tells a story, just like a movie

lessons.title: 13. Book: Height, width and depth

steps.say: The book gives a picture of a mix: a space with three directions. Height, width and depth.
Height is loudness: the louder part stands higher. Height is also pitch, from the deep bass at the bottom to the bright air at the top. A good mix fills every floor, and crowds none.
To check those floors, the book trusts your ears more than a picture of the frequencies on a screen. A screen can show a bump that is simply part of the music.
Width is panning, from far left to far right. The book counts panning among the strongest tools you have, and asks you to use the whole width.

Every CQ channel has a pan control. A start for Santoshi: Tajana, the bass and the mridangam in the middle. Svemir a little left, Igor a little right, so the two low male voices do not sit on top of each other. Snoopy's guitar to one side, Igor's guitar, DI and microphone, to the other. The djembe a little to the side, away from the mridangam.
Keep the two mridangam channels at the same pan. They are one drum with two microphones, the high head and the low head. Pan them apart and the drum breaks in two.

book.q: Small variations in panning can dramatically alter the sense of space within a mix.
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 2: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Five Best Practices › 2.1 Have a Concept

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Five Best Practices: Small variations in panning can dramatically alter the sense of space within a mix.
Depth is front and back. Two things make it: loudness, and how much room sound a part carries. A loud, dry part is close to you. A quieter part with more reverb steps back.

In Santoshi the three voices send about minus thirteen into the reverb, and the drums send nothing. So the voices have a soft room around them, and the rhythm stays dry and near. If a voice feels far away, try less reverb send before more fader.

lessons.title: 14. Book: Control the low end

steps.say: The book names the low end as the most common problem in mixes. There are two causes. Too much low on the bass instruments themselves. And too many instruments sharing the same low notes.

A surprise: adding low to a bass often makes it muddier, not bigger. What makes a bass clear are its overtones, the higher tones above each note. Our ears catch those easily, because they are close to the range of speech.

book.q: more bass doesn’t necessarily mean more apparent low-frequency information
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 3: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Four Common Mistakes › 3.1 Poor Control of the Low End

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Four Common Mistakes: more bass doesn’t necessarily mean more apparent low-frequency information

In Santoshi the low floor is shared by three: the bass DI, the low head of the mridangam, and the djembe. Listen to the three together. If they blur into one boom, take a little low away from one of them in its parametric EQ, the PEQ, instead of adding low to another.
To give the bass shape instead of weight, try a small lift in its overtones, somewhere around seven hundred to fifteen hundred hertz. Small moves, two or three decibels.
The book also says almost every instrument carries some low end, even the bright ones. Clearing the lows from many channels keeps the bottom clean. But not too much, or the whole mix turns thin.

On the CQ that is the high pass filter on each channel. The three voices already use it. Check the guitars next: a DI pickup often has a boom low down that adds nothing. Raise the guitar's HPF slowly until the guitar starts to lose its body, then go back a little.
The book warns that you can only judge the deep notes if your speakers and your room can play them. So learn how your own speakers sound in the low end, and judge the bass there.

lessons.title: 15. Book: Bright, but not too bright

steps.say: High frequencies are tempting. They make words clear and a sound present. A brighter sound is also louder, and louder always seems better. That is the trap.

book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 3: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Four Common Mistakes › 3.2 Overly Bright Mixes and Masters

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Four Common Mistakes: High frequencies are seductive.

The book describes two ways to use EQ. Cut what is too much, which sounds natural. Or boost what you want, which has more impact. Most engineers use both, but cutting is less likely to make a mix harsh.

Tajana's voice is high and already bright, so it needs little or no boost on top. Svemir and Igor are low voices. For them, first cut a little mud, around two to four hundred hertz, before you boost any presence.

The guitar pickups, the DI channels, can sound sharp at the top. Do not boost the guitars at the same height where the voices get their words. A small cut there on the guitars lets the words through, without the voices getting louder.

The mridangam's high head has a bright crack, and that is its character. But both mridangam microphones clipped at the concert. Boosting their top would make that distortion louder. Leave their highs alone, or cut a little.

One more point from the book. The sound that is best alone is not always the one that fits best in the mix. A guitar with a little less low and less presence may sound poorer alone, and better with the band.

So use solo to find a problem, with Live's S button, then turn solo off and decide with everyone playing. And when you compare before and after an EQ, remember a boost is also louder. Louder fools the ear.

lessons.title: 16. Book: Compression that keeps the music alive

steps.say: The book treats compression as a real help, and as a danger. Used gently, it keeps the important parts present without pushing their faders up. Used too much, it squeezes the life out of the music.
Voices and bass gain most from gentle compression. They carry the song, so they should not come and go. Done well, you hardly hear the compressor at all.

In Santoshi each voice has the Quick preset Vocal with Comp, and the bass has Bass Clean with Comp. Listen to a loud chorus: the voice should stay in front and still sound alive. If it sounds flat and pressed, the compression is too strong.
On drums compression can change the sound a lot. And a drum may pass through several compressors, one after another. Each adds a little, until the drums sound big at first and tiring after a while.
The mridangam and the djembe pass through two: their own preset compressor, and the glue on the main mix. That is enough. Over two hours of kirtan, the drumming should still breathe.
About the compressor on the whole mix, the book is clear. Keep the ratio low, and let it turn down only a few decibels, at the loudest moments.

book.q: Generally, buss compression should be at a fairly low ratio
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 3: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Four Common Mistakes › 3.3 Overly Compressed Mixes and Masters

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Four Common Mistakes: Generally, buss compression should be at a fairly low ratio
The Santoshi glue is one point nine to one, well inside that. On the loudest song, it should take away no more than three to six decibels.

And a tip on timing: switch the mix compressor in late. First make the balance right without it. If it is on from the start, you lean on it without noticing, and end up squashing. So next time, set the Main LR compressor out, balance, then switch it in for the last touch, and listen to what it adds.

lessons.title: 17. Book: How loud you listen, and how you compare

steps.say: The book says your listening level changes your decisions. Loud listening tires the ears quickly. And loud makes everything sound good, so you stop hearing what is wrong.

book.q: everything sounds better when it’s louder
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 2: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Five Best Practices › 2.2 Monitor Level

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Five Best Practices: everything sounds better when it’s louder
Start the day as quietly as is comfortable, because the level creeps up by itself. And at a low level you hear clearly what stands in front and what sits behind.
Use that for the voices. Turn the level down low and play Jai Ganesha. If you still understand Tajana's words over the drums, the voices are in front. If they disappear, they are too low.
Most of the work happens at a moderate level, because there the ear hears low and high most evenly. Loud listening is for the end of the day, for joy, not for decisions.
The book also says: choose one listening place and trust it. Other speakers, or the car, can wake you up to a problem. But the final decision is made on the system you know.
Comparing with music you love is a good guide: how loud is the voice, how bright is the whole, how wide. But no two recordings are alike. Use it as a direction, not as something to copy.

For Santoshi the best reference is the venue's own mix, on the USB channel. Press its listen key to hear it, release it to hear yours, in the same headphones, so the comparison is fair. If one is clearly louder, be careful: the louder one will always seem better.

lessons.title: 18. Book: Revise, rest, and know when it is done

steps.say: The book says that setting levels, pan, EQ, compression and reverb is only the beginning. Mixing is mostly revision: many small changes over time.
Listen in different ways. The whole piece from start to end. One section at a time. A few bars for detail. And each time listen for something else: the levels, the tone, the width, the depth.

Santoshi is two hours, eight songs. Use the markers to jump. Hear Jai Ganesha whole. Then the long Kali Kali, and the soft voice intro of Sarasvati Maha Lakshmi. The loudest and the softest moments test a mix the most.
Take short breaks, often. Fresh ears hear more, and the mind judges better early in the day. So do the most careful listening at the start of a session, and come back another day to check.
The CQ scenes make this easy. When you like a version, store it in a new scene slot, so Santoshi Mix stays as it is. Next day, recall it and listen before you change anything. You can always go back.
Play an unfinished mix only to the people who are part of it. The book's warning: others tend to love the first version they heard. Play it to everyone when it is done.

How do you know it is done? The book gives two signs. You only move faders by tiny amounts, a few tenths of a decibel. Or you listen with fresh ears and cannot decide whether it needs more work. And what bothers you today will be different tomorrow.

book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 2: Quick Guide to Great Mixes and Masters: Five Best Practices › 2.5 Live with Your Mix or Master

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Five Best Practices: don’t seek perfection (it’s not possible).

lessons.title: 19. Book: Setting levels, and the order of building

steps.say: The book says a mix depends on the arrangement. Parts that play in the same register fight each other. Parts in different registers are easy to mix. It calls this vertical arranging: everything that sounds at the same moment.

In Santoshi, Svemir and Igor are both low male voices, in the same register. And two guitars strum their chords right where the voices sing. That is where the work is. The bass, the mridangam and Tajana's high voice each have a floor of their own.
Horizontal arranging is the song along time. Find its high points and its quiet parts. A climax should stand out, but not be far louder than the rest. A soft intro may need help to keep up.

Many kirtan songs begin slow and soft and end fast and loud. Watch the end of each song on the main meter. And the soft voice intro of Sarasvati Maha Lakshmi, until about fifty minutes fifty four, may need a little more fader.
Build first the parts that are always there, then add the ones that come and go. The book brings the lead voice in early, because everything else is there to carry it.

book.q: everything ultimately is there to support and balance the lead vocal
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 4: Building a Mix: The Concepts and Tools in Detail › 4.1 Starting Concepts and Setting Level

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Building a Mix: everything ultimately is there to support and balance the lead vocal

For Santoshi: first the pulse that never stops, the mridangam with both heads and the bass. Straight after, the three voices. Then the guitars and the djembe, a step behind. Then the reverb. The earlier balance lesson started with the voices. The book puts the pulse first and the voices right after. Either way, the voices come in early.

Decide what stands in front and what stays behind. When every part pushes forward, the mix has no focus. In the book's example, moving the rhythm guitar and the harmony voice back opened the whole mix.

Watch the main meter while you build. With the main fader at zero, the book lets the drums alone peak around minus ten, to leave room for the rest. The finished mix should peak between minus six and minus three.

On the CQ: Main LR fader at zero. Bring up the mridangam and the bass until the main meter peaks near minus ten. When every channel is in, the loudest moment should sit between minus six and minus three. Too hot? Pull the channel faders down together, never the main above zero.

lessons.title: 20. Book: Panning in detail

book.q: Panning is the most neglected or underutilized element in many mixes.
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 4: Building a Mix: The Concepts and Tools in Detail › 4.2 Panning

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Building a Mix: Panning is the most neglected or underutilized element in many mixes.

The book's first rule: use the whole width, from hard left to hard right, and do not fear the edges. A part far out at the side is easy to hear; near the middle it blends. And keep the two sides in balance: an important part on the left wants a partner on the right.
Parts in the same register should sit far apart. Parts in different registers can sit close together.
Pan early. On most mixers a sound changes level when you move its pan, by a few decibels between the middle and the edge. Change the pans late, and your balance falls apart.
For two lead singers the book suggests a small offset, about fifteen percent left and right, and the same level when they sing together or take turns.
That refines my earlier suggestion. Svemir fifteen percent left, Igor fifteen percent right, Tajana in the centre.
For hand drums with a low and a high drum, the book puts the low one just off centre and the high one a bit farther out, on the same side. Hand drums seldom need the very centre.

The mridangam is one drum with two heads, so keep the two channels close, on one side. The low head about ten percent left, the high head about twenty five percent left. The bass stays in the centre. The djembe goes to the other side, about forty percent right.

The two guitars play the same chords in the same register, so they go far apart. Snoopy about seventy percent left. Igor's guitar seventy percent right, on the side of Igor's voice. Igor DI and Igor MIC get that same place.
Two rhythm guitars the book often pans fully hard left and right. When there are only a few parts in the mix, it pulls them in a little, to about eighty percent.

lessons.title: 21. Book: EQ in detail

steps.say: The book's main way to choose a frequency is to exaggerate. Turn one band up a lot, make it narrow, and sweep it slowly through the range. The bad spot and the sweet spot jump out at you.

On the CQ's PEQ: take a middle band, gain up to about plus twelve, width narrow, and turn the frequency slowly while the song plays. On Svemir, listen for the spot where the voice turns boomy or boxy. Remember that frequency.
Then the real move is small. Bring the gain back, and cut a few decibels at that spot, with a wider width. Wide curves and shelves sound gentler and more musical than narrow ones.
The book says the default shapes usually work: the top and bottom bands as shelves, the middle bands as bells of moderate width. Change them only for a reason.

The CQ's four bands work the same way. The lowest and the highest can act as shelves; the two middle ones are bells with a width control. For a voice: the low middle band for mud, the high middle band for the words, the top band for air.
A common shape is the smile: a little more low and a little more high. It makes up for our ears, which hear the middle best, most of all at low volume.
In Santoshi use a smile on one part at most. On every channel it would pile up the lowest notes and the sharpest highs, the two floors the earlier lessons keep clean.

book.q: Remember that there are no hard-and-fast rules (or presets!).
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 4: Building a Mix: The Concepts and Tools in Detail › 4.3 Processing: EQ

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Building a Mix: Remember that there are no hard-and-fast rules (or presets!).

That includes the Quick presets. Vocal Lo Pitch and Vocal Hi Pitch are good starting points, made for an average voice. Svemir, Igor and Tajana are not average: open each PEQ and fit it to that voice.

lessons.title: 22. Book: Compressor and gate, by source

steps.say: The book's usual starting point: a ratio between two and five to one, and a threshold where the loudest moments lose about six decibels. RMS detection follows the average and levels gently; peak detection catches every spike. A slow attack is gentle; a fast one tames spikes but can dull the sound.
Your Main LR glue uses RMS, the gentle way. On the channels the Quick presets chose the settings for you. Now you can read them with this in mind.
For a lead voice in a full band the book uses three or four to one, a fast attack, a soft knee, and up to seven to nine decibels at the loudest notes. Less when the music is sparse.
Santoshi is not crowded: three voices and a small band. Start lighter, around three to one, with three to five decibels on the loudest phrases. If a voice still jumps out, then more.

The bass wants a slow attack, fifty to seventy five milliseconds, so each note keeps its start. Its release follows the playing: long notes like a slow release, short notes a faster one. Acoustic guitars also want a slow attack, and when they are not the main part, a gentle ratio and only a couple of decibels.
So on Snoopy DI, Igor DI and Igor MIC: about two to one, two or three decibels, attack fifty milliseconds or more. The strum stays alive, and the guitars sit behind the voices.

book.q: Expanders have a much more limited role in mixing
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 4: Building a Mix: The Concepts and Tools in Detail › 4.4 Processing: Dynamics

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Building a Mix: Expanders have a much more limited role in mixing
A gate is the strong form of that: it turns the quiet moments down, or off. It is the opposite of a compressor, which turns the loud moments down.

So, a gate on the mridangam and the djembe? Mostly no. It would cut the soft ghost strokes and the ring of the drum, the life of a hand drum. Use one only where a channel is silent but noisy. Igor DI in the second half, after his guitar broke, is the clear case: if it carries hum there, a gate or simply its fader down removes it.

lessons.title: 23. Book: Reverb and delay in detail

steps.say: Reverb is a cloud of many reflections; a delay is one clear repeat. Reverb sounds natural and rich, but takes more space. A delay is a shortcut to space, but stark, and it can call attention to itself.

book.q: Don’t use a long reverb when a short reverb will do
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 4: Building a Mix: The Concepts and Tools in Detail › 4.5 Processing: Effects

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Building a Mix: Don’t use a long reverb when a short reverb will do

A short reverb is about one second or less, a long one one and a half or more. Parts in front can take a longer reverb; parts behind do better with a short one. Pick a preset that fits, rather than tweaking for hours. If it is wrong, try another preset.

Two settings deserve small moves. The time, until the tail breathes with the music. And pre delay: the short gap before the reverb starts. Twenty to forty milliseconds on a short reverb makes the room seem bigger without a longer tail.
On your CQ, the easy verb page shows only the room size and the type, and the manual names no pre delay control. So on FX1 you choose the type, Vocal Classic, and set how much each voice sends.
Delays must be timed to the music, so each repeat lands on the beat. Two or three repeats are usually enough.

Here kirtan is special: the tempo rises through each song, often a lot. A delay timed to the start is off the beat by the end. So for FX2, echo verb, either leave it off, or use a short slap of about one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty milliseconds, very quietly, on the voices only. A slap that short does not need to follow the beat.
To hear what an effect really does, stop the music and listen to the tail that is left. Then judge all the effects together the same way: the book calls this the delay pool.
In Live, solo Tajana with the S button and stop at the end of a phrase. On the CQ the reverb return keeps ringing her tail. That is her room.

lessons.title: 24. Book: The stereo buss, the last stage

steps.say: The stereo buss is the main mix, where every channel meets. The book calls it the border between mixing and mastering: whatever you do there touches every instrument at once.
On the CQ it is Main LR. Your glue compressor lives there, from the compression lesson. This lesson is about what else could go there, and what should not.

EQ on the whole mix is allowed, says the book, when it does something the channels cannot. A very gentle smile can be the finishing touch, or it can make the mix thin or boomy. Channel EQ is always the finer tool.
If you try it on the Main LR PEQ: one or two decibels at most, a low shelf and a high shelf. Switch it in and out at the same loudness. If you cannot hear a clear improvement, leave it out.

Reverb on the whole mix usually just muddies it. The book allows it only for a solo instrument or a very small group. It likes a touch of tube or tape colour on the buss, but not on a mix that is already warm.
Santoshi has ten channels, so no reverb on the main: the room comes from FX1, on the voices. And this warm, acoustic music needs no extra colour.

book.q: “Better” is the goal of the mix engineer
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 4: Building a Mix: The Concepts and Tools in Detail › 4.7 The Stereo Buss

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Building a Mix: “Better” is the goal of the mix engineer
For Santoshi there is no mastering after the SD card. What you hear on Main LR is the final sound. So make it right there, and keep the loudest peaks between minus six and minus three.

lessons.title: 25. Book: Mridangam and djembe

steps.say: The book says a drum set is many instruments in one. Work on each piece alone first, then make them play as one. Every drum has two parts: the attack, when the hand or stick hits, and the resonance, the ring of the body.
In Santoshi the drums are the mridangam, with one microphone on each head, and the djembe. The high head gives the sharp strokes, the low head the deep boom. Two sounds first, then one drum.
For hand drums the book lifts the very top, around eight to ten thousand hertz, to bring out the fingers, and the low middle to give the drum weight.

On the mridangam high head that top is where the strokes speak. But this channel clipped at the concert, and lifting its top lifts the distortion too. If you want more stroke, try a very small lift a little lower, around three to five thousand, and stop at the first harshness.

The deepest notes must be shared by the kick drum and the bass. The book gives the kick the very lowest area, around sixty to eighty hertz, and takes a little away from the bass there. Never boost both at the same frequency.

In a kirtan the low head of the mridangam plays the kick drum's role, and the djembe's bass tone joins it. Decide who owns sixty to eighty hertz: the mridangam low or the bass DI. Give it to one, and cut a little on the other with the PEQ.

book.q: Fast attack times will significantly dull the sound of drums and cymbals.
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 6: Mixing Piece by Piece: How to Approach Individual Elements › 6.1 Drums and Percussion

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Mixing Piece by Piece: Fast attack times will significantly dull the sound of drums and cymbals.
So on the compressors of all three drum channels, the attack should be slow: the first crack of each stroke passes before the compressor acts. If a stroke sounds dull, the attack is too fast.
Reverb on hand drums can work well, says the book. But pan the reverb with the drum, so it does not smear across the stage, and time it so it breathes with the rhythm.

On the CQ the reverb return is one stereo room for everyone; it cannot follow the drum's pan. That is one reason Santoshi sends no drums to FX1. If the drums sound too dry next to the voices, try a very small send from the mridangam high head only.

lessons.title: 26. Book: Bass DI and the guitars

steps.say: The book calls the bass perhaps the hardest part of a mix. It nearly always compresses it, because the bass is the floor the music stands on, and it should be felt all the time.
We hear the bass through its upper tones, around nine hundred to twelve hundred hertz. A lift there may sound odd alone and right in the band. The bass usually gets no reverb or delay.

Bass DI: centre, with its Quick preset Bass Clean and Comp. Attack fifty to seventy five milliseconds, so every note starts cleanly. Listen to how he plays: long held notes like a slow release, short notes a faster one. Ratio two and a half to four to one. On its PEQ, try a small bell near one thousand hertz: that narrows what the low end lesson suggested.

The acoustic guitar is where fits best is farthest from sounds best. In a full band it often needs a lot of low taken away and some top added to be heard. In a small group or a gentle style, much less of both.

Santoshi sits in between: two guitars, three voices, gentle music. So go halfway. A clear cut in the low middle, so the voices and the bass have room, and only a little top. The DI pickups are already bright; their top may need nothing.
The book notes that a pickup sounds thinner and brighter than a microphone on the same instrument. The microphone sounds fuller and more real.

That matters here. Igor played through his DI in the first half. After his guitar broke, a microphone on the new guitar, Igor MIC, took over. The two halves will sound different. Give Igor MIC more low cut than Igor DI, so his guitar sounds alike before and after the break, and the same pan for both.

book.q: Just because it was recorded doesn’t mean you have to use it.
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 6: Mixing Piece by Piece: How to Approach Individual Elements › 6.1 Drums and Percussion

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Mixing Piece by Piece: Just because it was recorded doesn’t mean you have to use it.
Igor DI is silent in the second half. Bring its fader down for those songs, or gate it, so any hum on it does not add up. A recorded channel plays only when it helps.

lessons.title: 27. Book: Three lead voices

steps.say: The voice is where every listener's ear goes first. The book keeps the lead in front and centred, but warns about the opposite danger too: a voice so loud that it seems to stand apart from the band.
When two lead singers sing in unison or take turns, the book sets them to the same level. When one sings the melody and the other a harmony, the melody sits slightly higher.

A high female voice and a low male voice are hard to balance, the book admits: they never sound equal. Its tools: soften the woman's presence a little, or lift the man's, and listen at very low and at fairly loud volume.

For Tajana against Svemir and Igor: try one or two decibels less around three thousand hertz on Tajana, or a little more on the men. Check at a whisper and at a fairly loud level, as in the listening lesson.

book.q: Compression is our friend but not our savior
book.from: Mixing and Mastering in the Box › Chapter 6: Mixing Piece by Piece: How to Approach Individual Elements › 6.5 Vocals

steps.say: The book says, in the chapter Mixing Piece by Piece: Compression is our friend but not our savior
Even well compressed, some words come out too soft or too loud. The book fixes them one by one, with automation.
On the CQ that is your hand. Ride the fader of whoever sings: a little up on a soft line, a little down on a shout. Compressor plus hand, the book's combination, played live.
A bright voice often sits well in a warm reverb, a warm voice in a brighter one. Harmony voices get simpler effects than the lead, often one small or medium room.
One FX1 serves all three voices. If Tajana's tail sounds sharp or hissy, lower her send a little. If Svemir and Igor sound too dry next to her, give them a little more send, not more fader.

Sharp s sounds are usually tamed with a de-esser, a compressor that listens only to the very top. The CQ channel has none. If Tajana's s sounds sting, take a small, narrow cut with the top PEQ band, around six to eight thousand hertz, only as much as needed.
